drills.q: Under the Poisson model, how does yield change with die area?
options: It falls with the square root of area
drills.why: Doubling the die does not halve the yield, it squares it. That shape is the reason a large modern part is several dies rather than one.

drills.q: What does the defect density D measure?
options: Fatal defects per unit area of wafer
The fraction of dies that fail
The number of process steps that can go wrong
drills.why: A particle, a misaligned layer or a random dopant fluctuation kills the die it lands on. The density is how often that happens per square centimetre.

drills.q: Which yield model does the industry use, and why?
options: Murphy, because it accounts for defect density varying across the wafer
Poisson, because it is the simplest
Seeds, because it is the most conservative
Whichever gives the best number for a press release
drills.why: Fitted to TSMC's 17.92 mm point, Murphy predicts their 100 mm point to within a tenth of a percentage point. That is a two-parameter model of where dust lands predicting a manufacturing outcome to three figures.

drills.q: Fitted to the same measurement, Poisson and Seeds predict what at 100 mm squared?
options: 28.8 and 41.8 per cent, against a measured 32
They cannot be fitted to a single point
drills.why: The models disagree by a lot at large areas, which is why the choice is not a detail. Seeds is not a bad model, it is a model of a differently behaved factory.

drills.q: At the reticle limit on a new process, a monolithic die yields roughly:
drills.why: Which is why a chip with two hundred billion transistors cannot be one piece of silicon. Not "would be expensive". Could not be manufactured.

drills.q: Why are chiplets used for large designs?
options: Four dies of a quarter the area each yield far better than one die of the
They allow mixing process nodes, and nothing else
drills.why: Four 200 mm dies yield 13 per cent each where one 800 mm die yields 1 per cent. The packaging and the interconnect cost power and latency, and it is still overwhelmingly the better trade.

drills.q: The edge correction in the dies-per-wafer formula accounts for:
options: Partial dies around the circular edge of the wafer, which cost
The area taken by test structures
drills.why: It is a second penalty on large dies, independent of yield and in the same direction. A big die is punished twice: fewer fit, and fewer of those work.

drills.q: What wavelength does extreme ultraviolet lithography use?
drills.why: A fourteenfold jump down in one step, and it comes with the problem that every material absorbs it, so there are no lenses and the whole optical path is in vacuum.

drills.q: How is extreme ultraviolet light produced?
options: Tin droplets vaporised into plasma by a two-pulse laser, fifty thousand
A solid-state laser at that wavelength
Filtered output from a mercury arc lamp
drills.why: There is no laser at 13.5 nanometres. The first pulse flattens the droplet and the second turns it into a plasma at half a million kelvin, which radiates at the right wavelength.

drills.q: Roughly what fraction of generated extreme ultraviolet light reaches the wafer?
drills.why: Every mirror returns about 70 per cent and there are eight or more in the path. That is why the source has to make hundreds of watts to deliver a few, and why the source is the hardest part of the machine.

drills.q: What does a node name like "3 nm" measure?
options: Nothing physical; it is a marketing label for a generation
The thickness of the gate oxide
drills.why: Until the 1990s the name tracked the gate length. Then they came apart. No dimension on a modern 3 nm chip is three nanometres, and different manufacturers' numbers are not comparable.

drills.q: What should you compare instead of node names?
options: Transistor density, cell area, drive current and leakage, which are
Marketing generation numbers, normalised per vendor
drills.why: Those are the numbers that decide what a design can do, and they can be measured rather than announced.

options: Sorting working dies by measured speed, power and functional
drills.why: A sixteen-core design with two bad cores becomes a twelve-core part. The consumer ladder is often not several designs but one design and a test result.

drills.q: A flagship graphics die with 192 processing units shipping 170 enabled is:
options: Yield harvesting, visible on the specification sheet
A software restriction that can be unlocked
drills.why: Those disabled units are the answer to a defect that landed somewhere. The same is true of a datacenter part with 144 units shipping 132.

drills.q: Why does the same design get cheaper over a process's life without changing?
options: Defect density falls by a factor of ten or more as the process matures,
Designs are re-laid-out for higher density
drills.why: About 1.27 defects per square centimetre during the ramp, and 0.05 to 0.2 on a mature process. It is also why the first parts on a new node are small ones: a manufacturer ramps on dies it can afford to throw away.
